events.title: Banks rescue a large investment fund
events.description: Private banks and securities firms invest in Long-Term Capital Management after heavy losses.

events.title: The euro begins
events.description: Eleven countries adopt a shared currency for financial transactions. Notes and coins come later.

events.title: The September 11 attacks
events.description: Terrorist attacks kill thousands in the United States. Communities mourn and help those affected.

what_happened_next.text:
Amazon led these choices, ending at about $3.32 per starting dollar. Apple ended near $1.45, and Microsoft near $1.11. Amazon’s route included very large monthly falls, and the final ranking hides how differently these investments felt along the way. The U.S. share basket and cash finished fairly close, while bonds did better than Microsoft.

Company events help make the period more concrete. In January 2002, Amazon reported its first small quarterly profit for the final quarter of 2001, on $1.12 billion in sales. Apple opened its iTunes Music Store on April 28, 2003; on May 5 it reported over one million songs sold in the first week. Microsoft said more than 67 million Windows XP licenses had sold by October 2002. Each business had a different kind of customer demand, but these facts cannot predict the stock’s full return.

The period also brought a rescue of Long-Term Capital Management, the euro’s start for financial transactions and the September 11 attacks, which brought devastating losses. Knowing that there was trouble at the start did not reveal which investments would recover. An exciting product or a frightening headline could sway a choice, but neither supplied a reliable five-year ranking.

reflection.what_people_were_focused_on: Russia’s financial crisis unsettled investors. Apple had a new computer, Amazon was adding music, and Microsoft faced a disputed antitrust case.
reflection.what_actually_mattered: The gains and losses along the way mattered as well as the ending value. One fast-changing company could create much sharper swings than cash.
reflection.what_faded_away: A product’s early sales and a legal headline did not give a complete five-year answer. No single story captured everything affecting a company.
reflection.what_nobody_knew: Nobody knew Amazon’s eventual result or the depth of the falls along the way. Its later fame can make a risky starting decision seem obvious in hindsight.

hot:1998-08:apple.text: Apple opened the iTunes Music Store on April 28, 2003. By May 5, the store had sold over one million songs in its first week, connecting Apple’s computers and digital music players with a new online music shop.

hot:1998-08:amazon.text: On January 22, 2002, Amazon reported a $5 million net profit for the final quarter of 2001, on $1.12 billion in sales. Amazon said lower prices and more product choices helped sales, marking its first profitable quarter under standard accounting rules after years of losses.

hot:1998-08:microsoft.text: By October 2002, Microsoft said more than 67 million Windows XP licenses had sold since the system launched in October 2001. The strong sales showed millions of customers were moving to Microsoft’s newest software for home and work computers.
